newsitem.title: USA: World Bank profit squeeze threatens aid to poor.
newsitem.headline: World Bank profit squeeze threatens aid to poor.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn was expected to warn economic policymakers on Tuesday that his organisation's net profits were set to drop sharply, leaving less money free to help the world's poor.

The warning, which Bank officials said would come on the final day of the lending agency's semi-annual meeting, would not be welcome news at a time when some Western governments are cutting back on aid to the developing world.

The Bank earned about $1.2 billion last year, which it used for a combination of purposes. Some was put into reserves. Some was used to reduce interest rate charges for borrowers or to help fund low-cost loans for the world's poorest nations.
The bank's profits are falling partly because it is earning less on the tens of billions of dollars it lends to developing countries and former Communist bloc nations each year.

The Bank has said it intends to use some of its future profits to finance its share of a new international plan to provide relief to debt-ridden poor countries which have followed tough economic plans from the International Monetary Fund.
Up to 20 countries are expected to qualify for help under the plan, which could cost creditors as much as $8.4 billion.

Developing nations, worried about falling levels of foreign aid, last week urged the World Bank and IMF to adopt more flexible terms for the new initiative, which will not benefit many poor countries for years.
But International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus rejected that call on Monday.

"We do not foresee any significant change of regime in the next few years. To have countries waiting for three or four years more to be at the completion point (when debt relief is actually granted) is not necessarily a catastrophe," he told a news conference. Camdessus said some 50 countries had already contributed around half the money the IMF needs to finance its share of the programme. He also defended the terms of the plan, which only applies to nations which have been carrying out tough reforms.

"Of course you could dream about a system where you forgive all the existing debt and not ask a country to apply adjustment programmes, but then you should prepare to go ahead with a new forgiveness of debt in 10 years," he said.
Foreign aid is under attack by voters in many industrial nations because of fears that it could be wasted on corrupt regimes in developing countries and the former Communist bloc.
To help allay those concerns, both the IMF and World Bank have stepped up their fight against graft.
"There have been four cases where (IMF) staff discovered cases of corruption which had a macroeconomic impact," Camdessus said.
He did not name the countries, but said the IMF had reacted by seeking strong steps from the governments concerned -- firing civil servants or setting up new tax and customs systems.
"Governments have cooperated and the situation has improved signifcantly in these four countries," he said.
